passage: Tanvir, you've gone quiet since you told me about that group chat, and I'm not letting it pass with a joke. Let your Usha Nani tell you something first. My first month in the women's hostel in Pune, the seniors pinned a drawing of me on the mess notice board every morning. My plaits, my village sari, a cow beside me. Everyone laughed. When I cried, they said, 'It's only ragging, yaar. Fun. Everyone goes through it.' I believed my hurt was the silly thing, not what they did. Then my roommate Farzana took me to the warden, Mrs Pinto. She looked at the drawings and said, 'This is not fun. This is humiliation, and it stops today.' Those plain words gave me my breath back. So now, beta, after dinner, you and I are calling your warden together, and then your mother.

qa.q: Where did the seniors pin the drawing?
qa.a: They pinned it on the mess notice board every morning.

qa.q: How did the word 'ragging' make Usha feel about her own hurt?
qa.a: It made her feel her hurt was silly and she was too sensitive, so she felt ashamed of crying instead of seeing the cruelty.

qa.q: What choice in the story changed things?
qa.a: Farzana took Usha to the warden, who named it humiliation and stopped it that day.

qa.q: How did Mrs Pinto see the drawings?
qa.a: She saw them as humiliation, not fun, and acted at once to stop it.

grounding: A grandmother recalls being mocked in a hostel and told it was only ragging, until an adult named the humiliation plainly, and acts the same evening for her grandson.

passage: It was the night before Samir's first semester exam, and the paying-guest house in Indore was loud with other boys cramming. His phone buzzed again: the batch group chat, another voice note mimicking his stammer, this one set to music. Forty-two laughing reactions. He sat on his bed with the chemistry book open and read the same line five times. Hemant, from the next room, leaned in. 'Bro, ignore it. It's just ragging. Fun. They do it to everyone.' 'Everyone gets a song about their stammer?' Samir said. 'It's not fun. It's mocking me, every day, in front of the whole batch.' Hemant went quiet, then sat down beside him. 'Okay. Then we tell someone tonight.' Samir called his faculty mentor with Hemant beside him. The mentor listened, asked him to save every message, and said the anti-ragging committee would have it before the first exam.

qa.q: How many laughing reactions did the voice note get?
qa.a: The voice note got forty-two laughing reactions.

qa.q: Why did Samir read the same line five times?
qa.a: He was hurt and humiliated by the daily mockery, and the pain made it impossible to focus the night before his exam.

qa.q: What changed when Samir named it plainly?
qa.a: Calling it mocking instead of fun made Hemant take it seriously, and together they told the faculty mentor that night.

qa.q: How does Hemant see it once Samir speaks?
qa.a: Hemant stops calling it fun, realises it is targeted mockery, and stays beside Samir while he reports it.

grounding: On the night before an exam, a student mocked in a group chat is told it is only ragging, names the harm plainly and reports it.

passage: The class group chat at the Chandigarh college had a new sticker: Gurleen's face from the orientation photo, cropped onto a cartoon of a village aunty with a milk can. It was the sixth one this month, and twenty people had replied with laughing faces. In the canteen, Divyansh slid his tray next to hers. 'Don't take it so seriously. It's college fun. Everyone gets ragged in first year.' Gurleen put down her spoon. 'Fun is when everyone's laughing. I'm not. This is people mocking me every week because of where I'm from.' Divyansh looked at his dal. 'I didn't make them.' 'You reacted to four.' He didn't answer. That afternoon Gurleen took screenshots of every sticker to her class mentor, Dr Bedi, who read them in silence and said, 'Thank you for bringing these. This is harassment, and it goes to the committee today.' That evening she called her mother and told her everything.

qa.q: What was Gurleen's face cropped onto?
qa.a: It was cropped onto a cartoon of a village aunty with a milk can.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen put down her spoon when Divyansh called it college fun?
qa.a: She felt hurt and angry that her distress was being brushed off, and she wanted the mockery named for what it was.

qa.q: What steps did Gurleen take that day?
qa.a: She named it plainly to Divyansh, took screenshots of every sticker to Dr Bedi, and called her mother that evening.

qa.q: Why might Divyansh insist it is just fun?
qa.a: Calling it fun lets Divyansh avoid feeling responsible for the four reactions he added and for the hurt it causes Gurleen.

grounding: A student repeatedly mocked in a group chat is told it is only college fun, names the harm plainly and takes it to a mentor the same day.

passage:
'So from next quarter we're rightsizing the support team,' Arohi said, clicking to the next slide. 'Streamlining for efficiency.'
Vijay raised his hand. 'Sorry, can I ask what that means in plain words?'
'It means the team structure becomes leaner.'
'Leaner how? What actually happens, and to whom?'
A pause. 'Eight roles will be removed.'
'Eight people lose their jobs.'
'Well, yes. Eight positions.'
'People,' Vijay said quietly. 'Rukhsana, Paul, the two night-shift guys. They have names. Do they know yet?'
'Not yet. Communications go out next week.'
'Then can we plan how they hear it? In person, with notice, with help finding other roles. Not an email with the word "rightsizing" in it.'
Arohi looked at the slide, then at him. 'That's fair,' she said. 'Let's add it to the plan.'

qa.q: How many roles will be removed?
qa.a: Eight roles will be removed.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling when he heard 'rightsizing'?
qa.a: Vijay felt uneasy and concerned, sensing the smooth word was hiding real harm to people he knew.

qa.q: How did asking 'What actually happens, and to whom?' help?
qa.a: It turned 'rightsizing' into eight people losing their jobs, which led to planning how they would hear it and what support they would get.

qa.q: How might Rukhsana feel if she learned about the layoff through an email saying 'rightsizing'?
qa.a: She would likely feel shocked and disrespected, as if she were a line on a slide rather than a person.

grounding: An adult hears a layoff called rightsizing and asks what actually happens to whom, bringing moral attention back to the people affected.

passage: At my first job, my manager Kiran had a word for everything. Staying till eleven was 'ownership'. Weekend calls were 'passion'. When Reshma cried in the washroom after a third late night, Kiran called it 'growth pains'. I went along with the words for months. Then one Friday Kiran announced, 'We're motivating the team with a stretch target: everyone stays till the release is done.' Something snapped into focus. I asked, 'What does that actually mean for people? How many hours, and who's covering Reshma's childcare?' The room went quiet. Kiran said, 'Eshaan, it's just a push.' I said, 'A push is fine. But if it means fourteen-hour days for two weeks, let's say that, and then decide if it's fair.' We ended up splitting the release into two phases. Reshma mouthed 'thank you' across the table. I realised how much the nice words had been doing our thinking for us.

qa.q: What did Kiran call staying till eleven?
qa.a: Kiran called it 'ownership'.

qa.q: Why did something 'snap into focus' for Eshaan?
qa.a: Eshaan felt uneasy and protective of teammates like Reshma, and the word 'motivating' finally seemed to be hiding exhausting, unfair hours.

qa.q: What did naming it plainly lead to?
qa.a: Saying 'fourteen-hour days for two weeks' let the team judge whether it was fair, and the release was split into two phases.

qa.q: How did Reshma experience Eshaan's question?
qa.a: Reshma seemed relieved and grateful, mouthing 'thank you', since Reshma's childcare had been ignored under the word 'push'.

grounding: An adult hears pressure called motivation and asks what it actually means for people, and the plain words change the plan.

passage:
Supervisor's note, regional office, Thursday.
In today's sales review, Yash presented his plan to 'motivate' field staff: a daily ranking of all thirty reps read aloud on the morning call, with the bottom five named. He called it healthy pressure. Aditi, who joined us eight months ago, asked to speak. She asked what would actually happen to the bottom five, day after day, in front of their peers. Yash said they'd work harder. Aditi said, calmly, 'Or they'll be embarrassed every morning, and some of our best people will leave. Can we call it public shaming and then decide if we want it?' The room went quiet. Several managers were nodding. We agreed to share rankings privately with each rep instead, with coaching for anyone struggling. I've asked Aditi to help draft the new approach, and I'll thank her in Monday's meeting.

qa.q: How many field reps would the daily ranking cover?
qa.a: It would cover all thirty reps.

qa.q: What does Aditi's calm tone suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt concerned for the reps but steady, wanting the plan judged by what it does to people rather than by its label.

qa.q: What change came from naming it plainly?
qa.a: Calling it public shaming led the meeting to share rankings privately with each rep, with coaching for anyone struggling.

qa.q: How would the bottom five reps have felt under the original plan?
qa.a: They would likely have felt embarrassed and discouraged every morning, named in front of their peers.

grounding: A supervisor's note shows an adult hearing public ranking called motivation and asking what actually happens to whom.

subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage: At recess in the government school at Meenangadi, Class 5 played seven-stones under the jackfruit tree. When Thomas ran over, Anitha said, 'No space. Go away.' Everyone laughed and turned their backs, and Reena turned hers too. Thomas stood there for a while, then went and sat on the steps alone. After school, when Reena's Amma asked why she was so quiet, Reena said, 'Thomas cried a little. But it wasn't me. Everyone told him to go. I only did what they did.' Amma put down the rice pot. 'So if twenty people turn their backs, it's nobody's back?' Reena frowned. 'It was mostly Anitha.' 'And whose back was yours?' Reena didn't answer. She was thinking about Thomas on the steps.

qa.q: Where did Class 5 play seven-stones?
qa.a: They played under the jackfruit tree.

qa.q: Why did Reena say 'I only did what they did'?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable and a bit guilty about Thomas crying, and sharing the blame with everyone made her part feel smaller.

qa.q: What could Reena do tomorrow?
qa.a: She could invite Thomas to play or sit with him, and say sorry for turning her back, instead of waiting for the others.

qa.q: What was recess like for Thomas?
qa.a: He was hurt and alone, sitting on the steps after everyone turned their backs, and he cried a little.

grounding: A child who joins in turning away a classmate says everyone did it, so her own part feels like no one's.

subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage: In the school canteen in Lisbon, the girls at Beatriz's table had a new rule: Noa couldn't sit with them anymore, because Marta said so. When Noa came over with her tray, everyone spread their bags across the empty chairs. Beatriz put her bag down too. Noa stood there holding the tray, then walked to the table by the bins. At dinner, Beatriz's father asked about her day. 'Noa cried at lunch,' she said, pushing peas around. 'But it's not my fault. Everyone put their bags on the chairs. I was just doing what the others did.' Her father waited. 'How many bags were on the chairs?' 'Five.' 'And whose was the fifth?' Beatriz stared at her peas. 'Mine,' she said, very quietly.

qa.q: Where did Noa go to sit?
qa.a: Noa walked to the table by the bins.

qa.q: Why did Beatriz say it was not her fault?
qa.a: She felt guilty about Noa crying, and since everyone put bags down, spreading the blame across the group made her own part feel less real.

qa.q: How did her father help Beatriz see her part?
qa.a: He asked how many bags there were and whose was the fifth, so she had to name her own action.

qa.q: What was lunch like for Noa?
qa.a: Noa was hurt and humiliated, standing with her tray while bags blocked every chair, and ended up crying at the table by the bins.

grounding: A child who helped block a classmate from the lunch table says everyone did it, until her father asks whose bag was hers.

subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage: At the summer camp run by the community centre, each cabin had to choose teammates for the treasure hunt. The girls from Cabin 3 agreed, in whispers, that nobody would pick Vasudha, because she was 'weird' and talked too much about insects. Zeenat didn't think she was weird. But when the counsellor asked who wanted Vasudha, Zeenat kept her hand down like everyone else. Vasudha was put with the counsellors' team. Later, at the water tank, the counsellor, Mrs Rego, asked Zeenat why nobody had picked her. 'Everyone decided,' Zeenat said. 'I didn't say anything mean. Nobody picked her.' Mrs Rego nodded. 'When everybody does it, each person thinks it was nobody. But it was nine hands staying down. One of them was yours.' Zeenat looked at her wet hands.

qa.q: Which team was Vasudha put with?
qa.a: Vasudha was put with the counsellors' team.

qa.q: Why did Zeenat keep her hand down even though she didn't think Vasudha was weird?
qa.a: She felt nervous about going against the group, and when everyone did the same, her own part seemed not to count.

qa.q: What could Zeenat do at the next activity?
qa.a: She could pick Vasudha or sit with her even if nobody else does, since one person breaking the pattern matters.

qa.q: How might Vasudha feel being put with the counsellors' team?
qa.a: Vasudha might feel lonely and embarrassed, noticing that no one her age chose her.

grounding: A child at camp joins the group in not picking a classmate and says everyone decided, until an adult points out her own hand.

subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage:
Tuesday
Mess today. On the school trip bus Kushal took a photo of Aparna asleep with her mouth open and a crisp packet on her head. He said, 'Send it to the class group, it's hilarious.' So I did. It's not like it was my idea. Kushal took it, Kushal told me to send it. I just happened to be the one with admin rights.
By lunch it had gone to three other sections. Aparna saw it and went into the girls' toilet and didn't come out for the whole period. Then Ms Rao called me and Kushal to the staff room. She'd already talked to Aparna. She made me delete it and asked who pressed send. I said Kushal told me to. She said, 'He asked. You chose.' She's calling Mummy tonight.
I still think Kushal should be in more trouble. But I keep seeing Aparna's face when she saw it.
Yash

qa.q: What was on Aparna's head in the photo?
qa.a: There was a crisp packet on her head.

qa.q: Why does Yash keep saying Kushal told Yash to send it?
qa.a: Yash feels guilty and defensive, and putting the decision on Kushal makes pressing send feel like someone else's act.

qa.q: What should Yash do next?
qa.a: Yash should apologise to Aparna directly, own that pressing send was a choice, and help make sure the photo is deleted everywhere.

qa.q: How did Aparna feel when she saw the photo?
qa.a: She was humiliated and upset, staying in the girls' toilet for a whole period.

grounding: A teenager who spread an embarrassing photo insists a friend told them to send it, while a teacher places the choice back with them.

subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage: At the tuition centre above the fertiliser shop in Karad, Ojas's phone buzzed during break. It was Dinesh, the oldest boy in the batch: 'Put that photo in the batch group.' The photo was one Ojas had taken by accident that morning: Sudha's maths test with a big red 12 on top, lying on the bench. He hesitated, then posted it. Dinesh said to, he told himself. By the end of break, Sudha was staring at her phone, her face stiff. She packed her bag and left before the second class. Kale Sir noticed the empty seat and asked what had happened. Nobody spoke, until Ojas mumbled, 'Dinesh told me to post something.' Kale Sir looked at him for a long moment. 'Dinesh gave an order. Your thumb pressed it. Delete it now, and you'll both apologise to Sudha. I'm calling her home and yours this evening.'

qa.q: What mark was on Sudha's maths test?
qa.a: There was a big red 12 on top.

qa.q: Why did Ojas tell himself 'Dinesh said to'?
qa.a: He felt uneasy about posting it, and putting the decision on the oldest boy made his own part feel smaller and less his fault.

qa.q: What did Kale Sir do that was wise?
qa.a: He made clear Ojas was responsible for pressing post, had the photo deleted, required apologies, and planned to call both homes that evening.

qa.q: How did Sudha feel when she saw the photo?
qa.a: She felt humiliated, her face going stiff, and she left before the second class.

grounding: A teenager who posted a classmate's embarrassing test paper says an older boy told him to, and a tutor places the responsibility back on him.

subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage: In the college library, Devika watched the hostel group chat fill up. Someone had posted Ojas's video from talent night, the part where he slipped mid-dance, with a caption comparing him to a buffalo on ice. Within ten minutes there were sixty replies. Memes. Voice notes of mooing. Devika's thumb hovered. There were two hundred people in that group. Surely one of the seniors would say something. Surely the admins would. Nobody did. Another meme. She thought of Ojas, who had fixed her laptop charger in the first week without being asked. She typed, deleted, typed again: 'This has gone past funny. He danced in front of three hundred people, which none of us did. Let's stop.' She pressed send and turned the phone face down, heart racing. When she looked again, two people had replied 'agreed', and an admin had deleted the video. She messaged Ojas privately: 'You okay? That was not okay.'

qa.q: What happened in Ojas's talent night video?
qa.a: He slipped mid-dance.

qa.q: Why did Devika wait before posting?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and nervous, assuming that with two hundred people in the group, surely a senior or an admin would speak up first.

qa.q: What made Devika's message effective?
qa.a: It was short and calm, said it had gone past funny, gave Ojas credit for performing, and asked everyone to stop, which let others agree.

qa.q: How might Ojas feel seeing the pile-on stop?
qa.a: He would likely feel relieved and less alone, especially after getting Devika's private message.

grounding: A student watching an online pile-on waits for someone else to speak, then posts one calm message that breaks the silence.

passage:
Subject: About last night

Tenzin,
I saw everything in the batch group last night. The edited pictures of you, the 'go back to your mountains' comments, the forty people laughing. I watched for two hours and said nothing. I kept thinking someone else would say something, someone closer to you, one of the class reps. Everyone probably thought that. So nobody did.
This morning I finally wrote in the group: 'Those comments about Tenzin are cruel and some are hateful. I'm not okay with it, and I'm reporting them to the class mentor.' Three people replied that they agreed. I've sent the screenshots to Dr Rao.
I'm sorry I waited so long. You shouldn't have been alone in that for two hours.
If you want company when you talk to Dr Rao, I'll come.
Avni

qa.q: How long did Avni watch without saying anything?
qa.a: Avni watched for two hours and said nothing.

qa.q: Why did Avni stay silent at first?
qa.a: Avni felt uneasy but assumed someone closer to Tenzin or a class rep would speak up, and since everyone thought the same, the silence felt shared.

qa.q: What did Avni's message in the group do?
qa.a: It calmly named the comments as cruel, said they were being reported, and three people then agreed, breaking the silence.

qa.q: How might Tenzin feel reading this email?
qa.a: Tenzin might feel hurt that so many stayed silent, but also less alone knowing someone spoke up and offered to come to Dr Rao.

grounding: In an email, a student admits staying silent during an online pile-on while waiting for someone else, then describes speaking up and reporting it.

subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage: You asked about a time I changed my mind, Divyansh. Here's one. Second year, our class group chat turned on a boy called Arun after he asked a question in a lecture that people thought was stupid. Someone made a sticker of his face. Then everyone did. For two days it was nonstop. I'm Maria, I'm usually loud, I argue with professors, and I said nothing. I told myself, it's a hundred people, somebody will stop this. I actually waited for somebody. On the third morning I saw Arun eating alone in the canteen, staring at his phone. I went back to my room and typed one line: 'Guys, he asked a question. That's what we're here for. Can we stop?' That's all. Within five minutes it went quiet. Someone even said sorry. One line. I still think about the two days I waited for somebody else to type it.

qa.q: What did Arun do in the lecture that started it?
qa.a: He asked a question people thought was stupid.

qa.q: Why did Maria, usually loud, stay silent for two days?
qa.a: Maria felt uneasy but assumed that among a hundred people somebody would stop it, so responsibility felt spread thin and belonged to no one in particular.

qa.q: What made Maria's one line work?
qa.a: It was calm and simple, pointed out that asking questions is the point of class, and asked everyone to stop, which gave others permission to go quiet.

qa.q: What were those two days like for Arun?
qa.a: Arun seemed isolated and hurt, eating alone in the canteen and staring at his phone while the stickers kept coming.

grounding: A student recalls watching a group chat humiliate a classmate while waiting for someone else to act, until one calm line from her ended it.

subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage: The truck for the Hyderabad order was due at the factory gate in two hours when Jyoti found it: the safety valves on batch 14 were sticking in the pressure test, eleven out of forty. She took the report to Farida, the production manager. Farida glanced at it. 'Mark the batch passed. We'll fix it in the next lot. If this order misses the truck, we lose the client.' Jyoti felt her hands go cold. 'I understand the instruction,' she said. 'But I'm the one signing the test sheet, and I'm responsible for what I sign. I can't mark it passed.' 'Then it's on you.' 'It is. That's why I'm raising it.' She emailed the quality head and the compliance officer with the test data, copying Farida. Within forty minutes the compliance officer, Mr Nair, came down to the floor himself, held batch 14, and told dispatch to send the other three batches on the truck.

qa.q: How many valves on batch 14 were sticking?
qa.a: Eleven out of forty were sticking.

qa.q: What did Jyoti feel when told to mark the batch passed, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt alarmed and tense, her hands going cold, yet she stayed steady in refusing.

qa.q: Why did Jyoti's response work?
qa.a: She acknowledged the instruction, owned her signature, and raised it with the quality head and compliance officer with data, so the right people could act.

qa.q: How might Farida feel after Mr Nair holds the batch?
qa.a: Farida may feel frustrated about the order but also relieved not to be responsible for faulty valves reaching customers.

grounding: Under time pressure, an employee told to pass a defective batch says she remains accountable for what she signs and raises it through proper channels.

subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage: In the glass meeting room of the startup's Koramangala office, Abhinav closed his laptop. 'Don't log that bug before Friday's demo. We'll quietly patch it next sprint.' The bug Devika had found let one user see another user's saved addresses. She took a breath. 'I hear you, and I get why the demo matters. But I'm the tester. If I find something like this and bury it, that's my choice, not just yours.' 'I'm the one telling you to.' 'You are. I'm still the one doing it.' That afternoon she logged it with a clear description and flagged it to the security lead, Sunita, as company policy asked. Sunita replied in ten minutes: 'Thank you. Pulling this into today's fix. The demo can use the old version.' Abhinav stopped by her desk later. He didn't apologise, but he said, 'Fair. Better now than in the news.'

qa.q: What did Devika's bug let users see?
qa.a: It let one user see another user's saved addresses.

qa.q: What does Devika's breath before answering suggest she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt nervous about pushing back on her manager but determined to stay honest.

qa.q: What did Devika do that shows owning the decision?
qa.a: She refused to bury the bug, logged it clearly and flagged it to the security lead as policy required, rather than hiding behind the instruction.

qa.q: How does Abhinav come to see her choice?
qa.a: He seems to accept it, admitting it is better fixed now than found later, even without apologising.

grounding: An employee told to hide a defect says she understands the instruction but stays accountable, and raises it through the proper channel.

'Just put the old labels on,' Hafsa said, stacking trays. 'Nobody's going to check.'
Afreen held up a packet. 'These have cashew in the filling now. The label says nut-free.'

grounding: An employee told to cover a labelling defect accepts she is still accountable for her own hands and raises it with the quality officer.

passage: In Nabha, the children of Mandi Lane never played with the children from across the canal. 'They're jungli,' Rehana told her little cousin, repeating what the older kids said. 'Dirty. They bite like dogs.' On Sunday the ball rolled over the canal bridge, and a girl from the other side, Gurleen, picked it up and held it out. Rehana snatched it and ran. 'Don't touch her, she's full of germs,' she shouted, and her friends laughed and threw pebbles at the bridge. Gurleen stood there, her hand still out. That evening Rehana's Nani, who had watched from the roof, called her up. 'What's that girl's name?' Rehana shrugged. 'One of them.' 'Go and find out tomorrow,' Nani said. 'You don't throw stones at someone whose name you know.'

qa.q: What did Rehana's friends throw at the bridge?
qa.a: They threw pebbles at the bridge.

qa.q: Why was it easy for Rehana to snatch the ball and shout about germs?
qa.a: Calling the other children dirty and like dogs made them feel less like real children, so being rough didn't make Rehana feel guilty in the moment.

passage: On Adeyemi Street in Lagos, the boys played football every evening in the gap between the parked cars. Emeka was the best dribbler, and he made the rules. Emeka's mother had seen it all from the balcony. At dinner she asked, 'Which wild animal gave you the ball back?' Emeka ate his rice and didn't answer. The next evening, he told Daniel he could play in goal.

Class teacher's note, Class 10, Friday.
In the free period I overheard Lalremsiami telling her group a joke about the construction workers in the sheds behind the school, calling them 'donkeys who can't count their own fingers'. The group laughed; Rashmi, beside her, added a braying sound. When I asked Lalremsiami about it later, she said it was just a joke everyone tells, and that 'they're not like us anyway'. I asked whether she knew any of them. She said no. I told her about Babulal, the mason who fixed our library roof last month, who has a daughter in Class 6 and sings while he works. She went quiet. I asked her to speak to one of the workers with me next week and write one paragraph about that person. She agreed. I've informed her mother, and I'll talk about the joke going round with the whole class on Monday.

qa.a: She called them 'donkeys who can't count their own fingers'.

qa.a: Seeing the workers as 'not like us' kept her from feeling empathy or guilt, so mocking them felt like harmless fun.

qa.a: The teacher described Babulal as a real person, arranged for her to speak to a worker and write about them, informed her mother and planned a class talk.

qa.a: He would likely feel hurt and insulted, having worked on their library roof while caring for his own daughter's schooling.
